youtube_title: The Contract That's Binding Before Your 'Yes' Even Arrives 🦝⚖️
caption: Under the mailbox rule, a properly sent acceptance can take effect when it's sent, not when it arrives — unless the offer says otherwise. Option contracts and state rules can change the result.
script: You can be legally locked into a contract before the other person even reads your answer. [disclaimer] It's called the mailbox rule! It's a basic rule of contract law in America. When you accept an offer, and you send your yes the right way, it counts the second you send it. Not when it shows up! The moment it leaves your hands, it's done. So picture this. Someone offers to sell you a machine, and on Monday, you mail back, yes, deal! On Tuesday, before your letter even gets there, they change their mind and try to take back the offer. Too late! Under the mailbox rule, you may already have a deal, because your yes counted when you sent it. So the person who made the offer takes the risk of slow mail. But here's where it gets messy. The rule only works if the offer doesn't say otherwise. The offer can say, your yes only counts when I actually get it. And option deals, where someone paid to keep an offer open, usually need the yes to actually arrive. Though some states see that differently. Courts have used this rule for things like email, but electronic messages raise their own questions, and the details change from state to state. So don't assume hitting send always makes a contract. [loop] So before you drop your acceptance in the mailbox, remember
